podcast.title: 1985 Concert Advertisement
podcast.body: A radio commercial from 1985 featured "38 specials" presenting a concert, described as "the strength of rock and roll back and back alive." This advertisement appeared alongside promotion for Honeymoon Suite. "The strength of rock and roll back and back alive in some concerts, present 38 specials."

podcast.title: Benefit from MTV
podcast.body: 38 Special significantly benefited from the advent of MTV in 1981. Their videos, particularly for "Hold On Loosely," received "regular rotation," which was crucial to their commercial success and ability to sell more records. "And they really did also benefit from MTV and getting their videos and regular rotation."

podcast.title: Distancing from "Southern Rock" Label
podcast.body: In 1986, during the "height of the arena rock, a hair band era," Donnie Van Zant stated that he considered the term "Southern Rock" to be "passé" and that 38 Special no longer wished to be associated with it. He expressed the band's desire to offer more than the stereotypical themes of "Cowboys whiskey, Alligators and bad women" often found in other Southern rock bands like Molly Hatchet. "We feel like we have more to offer than just some of the stereotypical Southern Rock bands that were singing about Cowboys whiskey, Alligators and bad women."

podcast.body: In 1986, during the height of the arena rock and hair band era, Johnny Van Zant stated that the term "Southern Rock" had become "rather passe." podcast.body: Donnie Van Zant is the brother of Ronnie Van Zant, the frontman of Lynyrd Skynyrd. This familial connection links 38 Special to one of the most prominent Southern Rock bands of the 1970s. "38 Special was Donnie Van Zantz Van Donnie was Ronnie's brother."

podcast.title: Influence of The Cars
podcast.body: To achieve commercial success, 38 Special "borrow[ed] a little something from the cars" for their sound, specifically drawing inspiration from the opening riff of "Just What I Needed" by The Cars (1978). This influence is discernible in their hit song "Hold On Loosely." "So one of the things that they tried was to borrow a little something from the cars. Does this sound familiar?"

podcast.title: Shift in Sound and Marketing Strategy
podcast.body: After their first two albums "failed miserably," 38 Special deliberately changed its sound, with Don Barnes focusing on writing songs "designed to get on the radio and this new thing that debuted in 1981 MTV." This strategic shift aimed for broader commercial success, moving away from their earlier Southern rock identity. "our first two albums failed miserably, and we started trying any kind of thing we could to win at this."

podcast.title: Sound Change for Commercial Success
podcast.body: After their first two albums "failed miserably," the band intentionally changed their sound, with Don Barnes beginning to write songs "designed to get them on the radio." This shift was a strategic move to "win," meaning to sell records and gain radio play. The emergence of MTV in 1981 further aided their efforts. "Don Barnes said our first two albums failed miserably and we started trying any kind of thing we could to win at this Winning of course meant selling records and getting on the radio."
